title: Exchanging self and other
hookLine: put others where you put yourself (Bodhicaryavatara 8)
tomorrow: patience, effort, quiet... all of it for what?

cards: Every home has a chair that belongs to someone. Dad's end of the couch. A grandmother's seat by the window.
Sit in it and the room changes: the TV from her angle, the version from the door she always mentions, the kitchen she keeps an eye on. A chair can hold a whole point of view.
Trading places for an hour sounds like a party game. Shantideva makes it a practice.

teach.b: He calls it the exchange of self and other, and he calls it a secret, a supreme one. Whoever wants to protect both themselves and others quickly, he says, should practice it. In Sanskrit, paratmaparivartana.
Here's the move. Equalizing said: we both want happiness.

teach.h: PUT THEM WHERE YOU PUT YOURSELF.
teach.b: Exchanging says: now put them where you usually put yourself. The care, the attention, the first serving that habit saves for me, give it to them, in the imagination first and then in small acts.
It's a practice for a bodhisattva, done with real faces.
Look out from their chair. Feel what they feel when plans change or the praise goes elsewhere. Then notice what happens to your own worries while you sit there: they get quieter.

teach.h: A CRAMPED ROOM GETS A WINDOW.
teach.b: A mind that thinks only of itself is a cramped room; the exchange opens a window. Shantideva doesn't pretend it's easy. It turns a lifetime's habit around.
Start small: one person, one hour, one chair.

how: Exchanging self and other is taught in Tibetan Buddhism as a core compassion practice, often linked with tonglen, a meditation of taking in others' pain and sending out ease.

games.q: what does “exchanging self and other” mean?
o: putting others where you usually put yourself
trading favors so that nobody owes anybody
pretending to be someone else to fit in

p: put them where you put yourself

s: Shantideva calls the exchange of self and other a supreme secret
whoever wants to protect self and others quickly, he says, should practice it.
the exchange means you stop caring for yourself at all
he offers it as a way to protect both self and others; your own worries get quieter, not ignored.

games.q: your little sister is upset at dinner, and you're tired. which move is the exchange?
o: sit in her place for a moment in your mind: what was her day like? answer from there.
tell her you had a hard day too, so you're even.
feel sorry for her quietly, but keep your plans for the evening exactly as they were.
games.why: the exchange puts her where you'd usually put yourself: her day first, then your answer.

practice: If you can, get up and walk to a seat someone else usually takes, at home or wherever you are; if you can't, walk there in your mind. Sit in it.
Look around from their angle, and name one thing they see every day that you rarely notice. Breathe there a while, as them.

wordCard.voice: Exchanging self and other: Shantideva's practice of putting others where you usually put yourself, in mind and then in act.

carryVoice: Your line: exchange. Their chair, and for an hour, your care. Forty days into the guide.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 8.120 and following (whoever wishes to protect self and others quickly should practice the supreme secret, the exchange of self and other)
